claim: Cells convert electrical signals into chemical outputs to facilitate the active transport of information across larger distances.
source: Cells convert electrical signals into chemical outputs to facilitate the active transport of information across larger distances.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular function presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: Electrical-to-chemical conversion requires a tightly regulated expression of ion channels.
source: This electrical-to-chemical conversion requires a tightly regulated expression of ion channels.
evidence: This is a general statement about ion channel regulation presented in the abstract.

claim: Alterations of ion channel expression provide landmarks of numerous pathological diseases, such as cardiac arrhythmia, epilepsy, or cancer.
source: Alterations of ion channel expression provide landmarks of numerous pathological diseases, such as cardiac arrhythmia, epilepsy, or cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established medical knowledge about ion channel-related diseases.

claim: The activity of ion channels can be locally regulated by external light or chemical stimulus.
source: Although the activity of ion channels can be locally regulated by external light or chemical stimulus, it remains challenging to coordinate the expression of ion channels on extended spatial–temporal scales.
evidence: This is a statement about existing capabilities in the field, presented as background knowledge.

claim: It remains challenging to coordinate the expression of ion channels on extended spatial–temporal scales.
source: Although the activity of ion channels can be locally regulated by external light or chemical stimulus, it remains challenging to coordinate the expression of ion channels on extended spatial–temporal scales.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current capabilities that the study aims to address.

claim: The authors engineered yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to read and convert chemical concentrations into a dynamic potassium channel expression.
source: Here, we engineered yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to read and convert chemical concentrations into a dynamic potassium channel expression.
evidence: This describes the main experimental approach of the study.

claim: A synthetic dual-feedback circuit controls the expression of engineered potassium channels through phytohormones auxin and salicylate.
source: A synthetic dual-feedback circuit controls the expression of engineered potassium channels through phytohormones auxin and salicylate to produce a macroscopically coordinated pulses of the plasma membrane potential.
evidence: This describes the mechanism used in the study, supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The synthetic dual-feedback circuit produces macroscopically coordinated pulses of the plasma membrane potential.
source: A synthetic dual-feedback circuit controls the expression of engineered potassium channels through phytohormones auxin and salicylate to produce a macroscopically coordinated pulses of the plasma membrane potential.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Electrical signals provide an active mechanism for the rapid delivery of information across noisy cells and tissues.
source: Electrical signals provide an active mechanism for the rapid delivery of information across noisy cells and tissues.
evidence: This is a general statement about electrical signaling in biological systems.

claim: Excitable neuronal circuits use electrical signaling.
source: Prominent examples of this phenomenon across kingdoms include excitable neuronal circuits (Aron and Yankner, 2016), plant defense signaling (Masatsugu, 2018), and metabolic coordination of biofilm growth (Prindle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aron and Yankner, 2016.

claim: Plant defense signaling uses electrical signaling.
source: Prominent examples of this phenomenon across kingdoms include excitable neuronal circuits (Aron and Yankner, 2016), plant defense signaling (Masatsugu, 2018), and metabolic coordination of biofilm growth (Prindle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masatsugu, 2018.

claim: Metabolic coordination of biofilm growth uses electrical signaling.
source: Prominent examples of this phenomenon across kingdoms include excitable neuronal circuits (Aron and Yankner, 2016), plant defense signaling (Masatsugu, 2018), and metabolic coordination of biofilm growth (Prindle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prindle et al., 2015.

claim: Different forms of electrical signaling involve ion channels.
source: These seemingly different forms of electrical signaling involve ion channels.
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of ion channels in electrical signaling.

claim: Outward-rectifying potassium channels release potassium from the intracellular reservoir to the extracellular space.
source: Outward-rectifying potassium channels release potassium from the intracellular reservoir to the extracellular space, thereby allowing for potassium exchange between neighboring cells (Debanne et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Debanne et al., 1997.

claim: Outward-rectifying potassium channels allow for potassium exchange between neighboring cells.
source: Outward-rectifying potassium channels release potassium from the intracellular reservoir to the extracellular space, thereby allowing for potassium exchange between neighboring cells (Debanne et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Debanne et al., 1997.

claim: A rapid gating of ion channels at the subcellular level maintains the balance in the plasma membrane potential.
source: A rapid gating of ion channels at the subcellular level maintains the balance in the plasma membrane potential (PMP), which is central to cell electrophysiology (Naundorf et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Naundorf et al., 2006.

claim: Plasma membrane potential is central to cell electrophysiology.
source: A rapid gating of ion channels at the subcellular level maintains the balance in the plasma membrane potential (PMP), which is central to cell electrophysiology (Naundorf et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Naundorf et al., 2006.

claim: The activity of potassium channels can be locally modulated by voltage-gating, mechanical or light stimulus, and external ligands.
source: The activity of potassium channels can be locally modulated by voltage-gating, mechanical or light stimulus, and external ligands.
evidence: This is a general statement about potassium channel modulation mechanisms.

claim: Advances in optogenetics and chemical biology of ion channels have powered numerous medical applications through local regulation of electrical activity in living cells.
source: In the last decade, advances in optogenetics and chemical biology of ion channels have powered numerous medical applications through local regulation of electrical activity in living cells with the ultimate goal of treating major life-threatening diseases (Gradinaru et al., 2010; Häfner and Sandoz, 2022; Snyder, 2017; Montnach et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: The spatial–temporal regulation of ion channel expression and membrane potential status is critical for landmarking pathological conditions such as cardiac arrhythmia, epilepsy, or various types of cancer.
source: Interestingly, recent studies indicate the spatial–temporal regulation of ion channel expression and membrane potential status is critical for landmarking pathological conditions such as cardiac arrhythmia, epilepsy, or various types of cancer (Rosati and McKinnon, 2004; Lastraioli et al., 2015; Zsiros et al., 2009; Niemeyer et al., 2001; Biasiotta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on ion channels and disease.

claim: A major challenge is to achieve rational control of ion channels on extended spatial–temporal scales.
source: However, a major challenge is to achieve rational control of ion channels on extended spatial–temporal scales.
evidence: This identifies a key challenge in the field that the study addresses.

claim: There is a lack of experimental models allowing a guided modulation of eukaryotic cell electrophysiology through modulation of ion channel expression.
source: Nevertheless, there is a lack of experimental models allowing a guided modulation of eukaryotic cell electrophysiology through modulation of ion channel expression.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current research capabilities.

claim: The authors built a synthetic gene regulatory mechanism capable of controlling ion channel expression in cell populations of Saccharomyces cerevisiae based on environmental changes.
source: To address this challenge, we build a synthetic gene regulatory mechanism that is capable of controlling ion channel expression in the cell populations of the model eukaryote Saccharomyces cerevisiae based on environmental changes.
evidence: This describes the main experimental approach, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The authors combined live-cell imaging in microfluidic devices with computer modeling to test a suitable eukaryotic model for macroscopic real-time modulation of ion channels and PMP in living cell collectives.
source: By combining live-cell imaging in microfluidic devices with computer modeling we tested a suitable eukaryotic model for macroscopic real-time modulation of ion channels and PMP in living cell collectives.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Chemical messengers or light can selectively control local activity of ion channels on the plasma membrane.
source: Chemical messengers or light can selectively control local activity of ion channels on the plasma membrane (Gradinaru et al., 2010; Häfner and Sandoz, 2022; Snyder, 2017; Montnach et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: The authors sought to implement an alternative system for ion channel modulation by chemically coordinating the ion channel expression at the macroscopic level.
source: In contrast, we sought to implement an alternative system for ion channel modulation by chemically coordinating the ion channel expression at the macroscopic level.
evidence: This describes the goal of the study.

claim: The authors previously developed a synthetic two component circuit to control gene expression across cell populations based on chemical stimulation with phytohormones auxin and salicylate.
source: Previously, we have developed a synthetic two component circuit to control gene expression across cell populations based on chemical stimulation with phytohormones auxin and salicylate (Pérez-García et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The circuit is composed of engineered Mar-type bacterial regulator IacR transcriptional activator and MarR transcriptional repressor.
source: This circuit is composed of engineered Mar-type bacterial regulator (Will and Fang, 2020); IacR transcriptional activator and MarR transcriptional repressor (Pérez-García et al., 2021; Figure 1A), that are inhibited by auxin (IAA) and salicylate (SA), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IacR and MarR are inhibited by auxin (IAA) and salicylate (SA), respectively.
source: This circuit is composed of engineered Mar-type bacterial regulator (Will and Fang, 2020); IacR transcriptional activator and MarR transcriptional repressor (Pérez-García et al., 2021; Figure 1A), that are inhibited by auxin (IAA) and salicylate (SA), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The circuit can coordinate gene expression in yeast on extended spatiotemporal scale.
source: We sought this particular circuit is ideal for our application since it can coordinate gene expression in yeast on extended spatiotemporal scale (Pérez-García et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The overexpression of potassium channel TOK1 in yeast leads to PMP hyperpolarization.
source: It is known that the overexpression of potassium channel TOK1 in yeast leads to PMP hyperpolarization (Sesti et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sesti et al., 2001.

claim: The authors used an open bacteria potassium channel KcsA* as the output module of the synthetic circuit.
source: Thus, we used an open bacteria potassium channel KcsA* (Doyle et al., 1998; Cuello et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2020) as the output module of the synthetic circuit (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The authors employed controlled conditions on the microfluidic chip where yeast can grow under continuous media perfusion stimulated with antithetic pulses of SA and IAA with regulable frequency.
source: To create a dynamic environment, we employed controlled conditions on the microfluidic chip where yeast can grow under continuous media perfusion stimulated with antithetic pulses of SA and IAA with the regulable frequency (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ThT outperforms other dyes (DIBAC4(3), DIS-C3(3)) in terms of stability, fluorescence level, low hydrophobicity, and near-linear response to potassium clamp experiments.
source: To monitor PMP changes we have tested several commonly used dyes in yeast such as DIBAC4(3), DIS-C3(3), and cationic dye Thioflavin T (ThT) (Peña et al., 2020) and we found that a ThT outperforms other dyes in terms of stability, fluorescence level, low hydrophobicity (Peña et al., 2020), and near-linear response to potassium clamp experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C and citation to Peña et al., 2020.

claim: The control strain that lacks the synthetic circuit does not show any regular changes in ThT fluorescence over time under coordinated changes of IAA and SA.
source: Under coordinated changes of IAA and SA in the environment, the control strain that lacks the synthetic circuit (Figure 1A) does not show any regular changes in ThT fluorescence over time (Figure 1D, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E and supplementary figures.

claim: The open-loop circuit driving KcsA channel in yeast showed noisy but recognizable fluctuations of ThT fluorescence with weak coupling between colonies.
source: Whereas the open-loop circuit driving KcsA channel in yeast (Figure 1A, B) showed noisy but recognizable fluctuations of ThT fluorescence with weak coupling between colonies detected by cumulative autocorrelation analysis (Figure 1F, G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F, G and supplementary figures.

claim: The period of ThT fluorescence showed a broad distribution around the phytohormone stimuli period in the open-loop circuit.
source: The period of ThT fluorescence showed a broad distribution around the phytohormone stimuli period (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and supplementary figures.

claim: Around 50% yeast colonies show synchronicity of ThT fluorescence in the open-loop system.
source: Notably, we found that around 50% yeast colonies show synchronicity of ThT fluorescence (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The open-loop system does not provide sufficiently robust changes in PMP to guide electrical activity on the macroscopic scale.
source: Based on these data, we concluded that this open-loop system does not provide sufficiently robust changes in PMP to guide electrical activity on the macroscopic scale.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on the open-loop system.

claim: The authors coupled IacR and MarR through positive and negative feedback loops in the dual-feedback synthetic gene circuit.
source: For that we coupled IacR and MarR through positive and negative feedback loops in the dual-feedback synthetic gene circuit (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the design of the improved circuit shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Computer model simulations of the IacR–MarR feedback system identified regimes that demonstrate the prominence for the excitable dynamics.
source: To analyze the robustness and dynamics of the designed circuit we first performed computer model simulations of this IacR–MarR feedback system and identified regimes that demonstrate the prominence for the excitable dynamics (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: Model predictions revealed minimal prerequisites for the transit between steady state, excitability, and oscillations.
source: Model predictions revealed minimal prerequisites for the transit between steady state (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), excitability (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and oscillations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: The conditions for transit between steady state, excitability, and oscillations directly relate to the ratio of IacR–MarR deactivation which depends primarily on IAA and SA changes.
source: These conditions directly relate to the ratio of IacR–MarR deactivation which depends primarily on IAA and SA changes (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: The dual-feedback circuit responds sharply to SA–IAA gradient and shows excitable-like dynamics characterized by transient response peak in the absence of periodic hormone stimulus.
source: We found that this dual-feedback circuit responds sharply to SA–IAA gradient and shows excitable-like dynamics characterized by transient response peak in the absence of periodic hormone stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Long step-like stimulation with IAA in dynamic microfluidic setup resulted in refractory dynamics of dEGFP signal after IAA removal.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that the long step-like stimulation with IAA in dynamic microfluidic setup resulted in refractory dynamics of dEGFP signal after IAA removal (Figure 2C), characterized by transient response peak similar to that observed in the static environment (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and in our computer model simulations (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claim: Spatially coordinated pulses of dEGFP were observed under various phytohormone stimulations of 2 hr, 1 hr, and 30 min.
source: Next, we impose cyclic applications of IAA and SA with defined periods to guide gene expression patterns across yeast colonies. Spatially coordinated pulses of dEGFP were observed under various phytohormone stimulations of 2 hr, 1 hr, and 30 min (Figure 2E, F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—video 1) which are in a good agreement with computer model simulations (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, F and supplementary figures.

claim: The observed dEGFP dynamics are in good agreement with computer model simulations.
source: Spatially coordinated pulses of dEGFP were observed under various phytohormone stimulations of 2 hr, 1 hr, and 30 min (Figure 2E, F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—video 1) which are in a good agreement with computer model simulations (Figure 2D).
evidence: This compares experimental data with computational predictions.

claim: Approximately 95% of all communities show coordinated peaks of dEGFP fluorescence.
source: Importantly, we quantified that ~95% of all communities show coordinated peaks of dEGFP fluorescence (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Phytohormone stimuli lead to coordinated spikes of KcsA-EGFP fluorescence mimicking that of dEGFP fluorescent marker.
source: Indeed, phytohormone stimuli lead to coordinated spikes of KcsA-EGFP fluorescence mimicking that of dEGFP fluorescent marker, indicating that our circuit specifically controls the amount of heterologous ion channels inside the cell under guidance of phytohormones (Figure 2—figure supplement 7, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The circuit specifically controls the amount of heterologous ion channels inside the cell under guidance of phytohormones.
source: Indeed, phytohormone stimuli lead to coordinated spikes of KcsA-EGFP fluorescence mimicking that of dEGFP fluorescent marker, indicating that our circuit specifically controls the amount of heterologous ion channels inside the cell under guidance of phytohormones (Figure 2—figure supplement 7, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the KcsA-EGFP fluorescence data.

claim: The chemically excited circuit presents a plausible regulatory module for engineering macroscopically coordinated ion channel expression in yeast cell populations.
source: In summary, this chemically excited circuit presents a plausible regulatory module for engineering macroscopically coordinated ion channel expression in yeast cell populations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: The dual-feedback circuit shows characteristics of excitable system that robustly controls the ion channel expression in yeast cell collectives.
source: We have demonstrated that dual-feedback circuit shows characteristics of excitable system that robustly controls the ion channel expression in yeast cell collectives.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the dual-feedback circuit experiments.

claim: Cyclic bursts of ThT fluorescence were remarkably consistent across cell populations in long-term experiments with the dual-feedback circuit.
source: Next, we grew engineered yeasts carrying a dual-feedback circuit in the microfluidic device that was subjected to different frequencies of SA and IAA stimuli (3, 2, and 1 hr, respectively). We could observe cyclic bursts of ThT fluorescence that were remarkably consistent across cell populations in long-term experiments (Figure 3A, B, and Figure 3—videos 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Cumulative autocorrelation and synchronicity analyses confirmed the robustness of temporal response on the macroscopic scale.
source: Cumulative autocorrelation and synchronicity analyses confirmed further the robustness of temporal response on the macroscopic scale (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D.

claim: The faster pace of environmental changes led to somehow less robust response possibly due to toxic effect of upregulation ion channels in short time periods.
source: The faster pace of environmental changes led to somehow less robust response possibly due to toxic effect of upregulation ion channels in short time periods (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary figures.

claim: While peak width and period were very consistent between different yeast colonies, there was visible variation in amplitudes of ThT fluorescence.
source: Interestingly, while peak width and period were very consistent between different yeast colonies, we observed visible variation in amplitudes of ThT fluorescence (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Variation in ThT fluorescence amplitudes could be due to subtle differences in relative levels of KcsA* channels produced by each cell or to inherent noise nature of gene expression.
source: These could be due to subtle differences in relative levels of KcsA* channels produced by each cell as observed in our experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 7) but also to inherent noise nature of gene expression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed variation in amplitudes.

claim: Dual-feedback integration in the original open-loop circuit significantly improves the robustness of ion channel control, resulting in coordinated modulation of ion channel expression and consequently organized changes of PMP across eukaryotic cell communities.
source: Nevertheless, our experiments indicate that dual-feedback integration in our original open-loop circuit significantly improves the robustness of ion channel control, resulting in coordinated modulation of ion channel expression and consequently organized changes of PMP across eukaryotic cell communities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing open-loop and closed-loop circuit performance.

claim: The PMP of yeast is regulated through voltage-gated potassium channels such as the outward-rectifier channel TOK1.
source: The PMP of yeast is regulated through voltage-gated potassium channels such as the outward-rectifier channel TOK1 (Martinac et al., 2008; Mackie and Brodsky, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martinac et al., 2008 and Mackie and Brodsky, 2018.

claim: TOK1 is the main target for several toxins and volatile anesthetic agents.
source: TOK1 is the main target for several toxins and volatile anesthetic agents (Ahmed et al., 1999), which cause uncontrolled opening and leakage of potassium ions to the extracellular space.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahmed et al., 1999.

claim: Toxins and volatile anesthetic agents cause uncontrolled opening and leakage of potassium ions to the extracellular space through TOK1.
source: TOK1 is the main target for several toxins and volatile anesthetic agents (Ahmed et al., 1999), which cause uncontrolled opening and leakage of potassium ions to the extracellular space.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahmed et al., 1999.

claim: Overexpression of TOK1 causes membrane hyperpolarization (more negative PMP).
source: Overexpression of TOK1 causes membrane hyperpolarization (more negative PMP) while tok1 mutation leads to membrane depolarization often accompanied by cell death (Sesti et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sesti et al., 2001.

claim: tok1 mutation leads to membrane depolarization often accompanied by cell death.
source: Overexpression of TOK1 causes membrane hyperpolarization (more negative PMP) while tok1 mutation leads to membrane depolarization often accompanied by cell death (Sesti et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sesti et al., 2001.

claim: TOK1 controls potassium release from yeast cells and maintains a balance in the PMP.
source: Thereby, TOK1 controls potassium release from yeast cells and maintains a balance in the PMP.
evidence: This is a statement about TOK1 function based on cited literature.

claim: The authors constructed TOK1* channel by tagging degron domain at c-terminus of TOK1 to decrease half-life of the channel and increase its dynamics.
source: For that purpose, we constructed TOK1* channel by tagging degron domain at c-terminus of TOK1 to decrease half-life of the channel and thus increase its dynamics similar to that of KcsA* construction.
evidence: This describes the construction of the TOK1* channel.

claim: Phytohormone stimuli lead to consistent ThT pulses across number of independent yeast colonies with TOK1* channel.
source: We recorded ThT fluorescence changes over time under pulses of IAA and SA. Similarly, to KcsA* we observed consistent ThT pulses across number of independent yeast colonies (Figure 3G, H, Figure 3—video 4) as exemplified by persistence of pulsing period and synchronicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G, H and supplementary figures.

claim: The dual-feedback circuit can control the expression of native channels to modulate its activity by controlling the number of TOK1* transcripts available in the cell.
source: These data indicate that our dual-feedback circuit can indeed control also the expression of native channels to modulate its activity by controlling the number of TOK1* transcripts available in the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TOK1* experimental data.

claim: The findings highlight a generality of strategy that includes engineered dual-feedback system for controlling potassium channels and PMP through environmental rhythms.
source: Therefore, our findings highlight a generality of strategy that includes engineered dual-feedback system for controlling potassium channels and PMP through environmental rhythms.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the generality of the approach based on both KcsA* and TOK1* results.

claim: In the last decade, many efforts have been invested into developing new methods for the local control of ion channel activity with light or chemical signals.
source: In the last decade, many efforts have been invested into developing new methods for the local control of ion channel activity with light or chemical signals.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: Mechanisms controlling ion channel expression have received substantially less attention, despite their importance in cardiac, neurological disorders and various forms of cancer.
source: In contrast, mechanisms controlling ion channel expression have received substantially less attention, despite their importance in cardiac, neurological disorders and various forms of cancer.
evidence: This identifies a gap in research focus.

claim: The authors demonstrate a synthetic biology model for the control of potassium channel expression on macroscopic scales in eukaryotic cell populations.
source: Here, we demonstrate a synthetic biology model for the control of potassium channel expression on macroscopic scales in eukaryotic cell populations.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the study.

claim: A synthetic gene circuit controls ion channel dosage in each individual cell that is dictated by environmental input with selective frequencies.
source: We demonstrated that a synthetic gene circuit controls ion channel dosage in each individual cell that is dictated by environmental input with selective frequencies.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Changes in ion channel expression correlate with changes of PMP as shown by cationic dye translocation to the cell interior with increased fluorescence.
source: Changes in ion channel expression correlate with changes of PMP as shown by cationic dye translocation to the cell interior with increased fluorescence.
evidence: This is a summary of the relationship between ion channel expression and PMP changes.

claim: Both heterologous and native channels were used as effectors of dual-feedback system to control PMP in yeast cells.
source: Both heterologous and native channels were used as effectors of dual-feedback system to control PMP in yeast cells.
evidence: This summarizes the use of both KcsA* and TOK1* channels.

claim: The lack of feedback causes a noisy control of PMP.
source: Whereas the lack of feedback causes a noisy control of PMP, highlighting strong benefits of using dual-feedback regulation for the robust PMP control.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing open-loop and closed-loop systems.

claim: Dual-feedback regulation provides strong benefits for robust PMP control.
source: Whereas the lack of feedback causes a noisy control of PMP, highlighting strong benefits of using dual-feedback regulation for the robust PMP control.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing open-loop and closed-loop systems.

claim: This work opens new avenues in the field of synthetic biology and cellular engineering by enabling a transformation of clocked chemical cues into coordinated ion channel expression without need for apparent cell-to-cell coupling.
source: This work opens new avenues in the field of synthetic biology and cellular engineering by enabling a transformation of clocked chemical cues into coordinated ion channel expression without need for apparent cell-to-cell coupling.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of the work.

claim: Coherent changes of ion channel expression can adjust electrical activity in growing cell populations and on extended spatial–temporal scales.
source: Our work proposes that coherent changes of ion channel expression can adjust electrical activity in growing cell populations and on extended spatial–temporal scales.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: The circuit could be potentially plugged into native context where timed processes would control circuit components endogenously and connect circuit output to native ion channel dosage.
source: Furthermore, our circuit could be potentially plugged into native context where timed processes would control circuit components endogenously and connect circuit output to native ion channel dosage.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: The initial, proof-of-concept study produces some variability in response amplitudes.
source: Nevertheless, our initial, proof-of-concept study produces some variability in response amplitudes.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: Future studies are needed to establish systems with improved response robustness to timed inputs.
source: Therefore, future studies are needed to establish systems with improved response robustness to timed inputs, potentially leading to the creation of powerful toolboxes for controlling macroscopic electrophysiology across the tree of life.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Controlling locally and globally ion channel expression holds a key to designing more effective therapies providing the control of electrical status of abnormal cells in a broad spectrum of diseases.
source: Practically, controlling locally and globally ion channel expression holds a key to designing more effective therapies providing the control of electrical status of abnormal cells in a broad spectrum of diseases.
evidence: This is a statement about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: A middle-copy episomal plasmid pGADT7 was used to increase the concentration of proteins to buffer for the effects of intrinsic molecular noise.
source: A middle-copy (~10–30 copies) episomal plasmid pGADT7 (Takara Bio Inc) was used to increase the concentration of proteins to buffer for the effects of intrinsic molecular noise and selected using different auxotrophic selection markers (Leucine, Uracil, and Histidine).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the experimental design.

claim: MarR, IacR, and KcsA* were codon optimized for yeast and synthesized using services delivered by Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT).
source: MarR, IacR, and KcsA* were codon optimized for yeast and synthesized using services delivered by Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT).
evidence: This describes the construction of key components.

claim: KcsA bacterial potassium channel was engineered to include open configuration mutations as previously described.
source: KcsA bacterial potassium channel was engineered to include open configuration mutations as previously described (Cuello et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2020) and modified further to include plasma membrane localization signals and c-terminus mouse ODC degron signal (Takeuchi et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the engineering of the KcsA channel, supported by citations.

claim: The BY4741 laboratory yeast strain carrying integrated copy constitutively expressed mCherry reporter was used to prepare competent cells and transformation of plasmids.
source: The BY4741 laboratory yeast strain (a kind gift from Dr. Luis Rubio) carrying integrated copy constitutively expressed mCherry reporter was used to prepare competent cells and transformation of plasmids using Frozen-EZ Yeast Transformation II Kit (Zymo Research).
evidence: This describes the yeast strain used in the study.

claim: Thioflavin T shows a near-linear drop in fluorescence after excessive amounts of potassium have been applied.
source: Note, a near-linear drop in ThT fluorescence after excessive amounts of potassium have been applied.
evidence: This is noted in the description of Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: DIBAC4(3) and Dis-C3(3) show low signal after 24 hr (low stability) and more exponential decaying trend (lower dynamic range) compared to ThT.
source: Other two commonly used PMP dyes show low signal after 24 hr (low stability) and more exponential decaying trend (lower dynamic range).
evidence: This is noted in the description of Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Each cell trap is 500 × 500 × 7 μm size, hosting ~10,000 haploid yeast cells.
source: Each cell trap is 500 × 500 × 7 μm size, hosting ~10,000 haploid yeast cells.
evidence: This describes the dimensions of the microfluidic device traps.

claim: Flow channels widths were 120 μm in the mixer module and 500 μm in main channels.
source: Flow channels widths were 120 μm for in the mixer module and 500 μm in main channels.
evidence: This describes the microfluidic device dimensions shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The approximate height of channels was 25 μm.
source: The approximate height of channels was 25 μm.
evidence: This describes the microfluidic device dimensions shown in Figure 1C.

claim: KcsA* contains plasma membrane localization (PM loc) and c-terminus mouse ODC degron sequences.
source: KcsA* contains plasma membrane localization (PM loc, green) and c-terminus mouse ODC degron (degron, black) sequences.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Activator IacR and repressor MarR are induced by galactose and repressed by auxin and salicylate, respectively.
source: Activator IacR and repressor MarR (tagged with ODC degron; Takeuchi et al., 2008) are induced by galactose and repressed by auxin and salicylate, respectively (Pérez-García et al., 2021).
